---
title: "Power"
date: 2026-11-13
type: essay
description: "How large a trial needs to be, where the sample size formula comes from, and why significant results from small trials tend to be too large."
categories: [statistics]
---

How many patients does a trial need? Most trial protocols answer this in a short paragraph that few people read. The paragraph matters more than it looks, because the same calculation tells us how to read a negative result, and why positive results from small trials are usually too optimistic.

We will use one example throughout. A new drug is compared with placebo for preventing stroke over five years. Suppose the true risk of stroke is 10% on placebo and 8% on the drug. The true risk difference is then

$$
\delta = p_1 - p_2 = 0.10 - 0.08 = 0.02,
$$

or two percentage points.

A trial with $n$ patients in each arm estimates $\delta$ by the difference between the two observed proportions, $\hat\delta = \hat p_1 - \hat p_2$. This estimate will not be exactly 0.02. If we ran the same trial many times, the estimates would scatter around 0.02, and for trials of reasonable size the scatter is close to a normal distribution:

$$
\hat\delta \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\delta,\; \mathrm{SE}^2\right), \qquad
\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)}{n}}.
$$

The standard error, SE, is the typical size of the error in a single trial.[^var] In our example $p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2) = 0.09 + 0.0736 = 0.1636$. With 2,000 patients per arm,

$$
\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{0.1636 / 2000} \approx 0.0090,
$$

a little under one percentage point. Note that $n$ appears under a square root. A trial four times as large has half the error, not a quarter.

Now we need a rule for deciding whether the drug works. The usual rule asks whether the observed difference is larger than chance would often produce if the drug did nothing. At a two-sided significance level of 5%, we call the result significant if

$$
\left| \frac{\hat\delta}{\mathrm{SE}} \right| > 1.96.
$$

The number 1.96 is chosen because a standard normal variable exceeds it only 2.5% of the time in each direction. Put another way, the observed difference has to be larger than

$$
c = 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}.
$$

With 2,000 per arm, $c \approx 0.0177$. The trial needs to observe a difference of about 1.8 percentage points or more.

Power is the probability that the trial is significant, given that the drug really works. We know $\hat\delta$ is centred on $\delta$ with standard deviation SE, so the probability that it lands above $c$ is

$$
\text{power} \approx \Phi\!\left( \frac{\delta}{\mathrm{SE}} - 1.96 \right),
$$

where $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal.[^tail] The only thing that matters is the ratio $\delta/\mathrm{SE}$, the size of the true effect relative to the size of the error. For 2,000 per arm, $\delta/\mathrm{SE} = 0.02/0.0090 \approx 2.21$, so

$$
\text{power} \approx \Phi(2.21 - 1.96) = \Phi(0.25) \approx 0.60.
$$

So a trial of 4,000 patients, testing a drug that does prevent strokes, has only a 60% chance of showing it.

We can turn this around to find the sample size. For power $1-\beta$, we need the quantity inside $\Phi$ to equal $z_{1-\beta}$, the point with probability $1-\beta$ below it. For 80% power, $z_{0.8} \approx 0.84$. Setting $\delta/\mathrm{SE} - 1.96 = 0.84$, substituting for SE and solving for $n$ gives the familiar formula

$$
n = \frac{\left(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}\right)^2 \left[\, p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2) \,\right]}{\delta^2}.
$$

In our example,

$$
n = \frac{(1.96 + 0.84)^2 \times 0.1636}{0.02^2} \approx 3{,}210
$$

per arm. The trial of 2,000 per arm was too small for 80% power.

The $\delta^2$ in the denominator is worth dwelling on. The required size depends on the inverse square of the effect:

| True risk difference | Patients per arm for 80% power |
|---|---|
| 4 percentage points | about 800 |
| 2 percentage points | about 3,200 |
| 1 percentage point | about 12,800 |

If the effect is half as large, the trial must be four times as large. Many treatments have small absolute effects, which is why convincing trials of them are large. It also means that a trial planned around an optimistic guess at the effect will have much less power than intended if the real effect is smaller.

What does low power mean for reading a result? Take the negative case first. If our trial of 2,000 per arm finds no significant difference, we should not conclude that the drug does not work. A drug that does work would give this result 40% of the time. The confidence interval shows this more clearly than the p-value. A non-significant result from this trial might have an interval of $-0.002$ to $0.033$, which includes no effect but also includes effects larger than the true one.

The positive case is less obvious. Suppose a trial is significant. Its estimate must have landed above $c$, so the significant trials are a selected group: the ones where the estimate happened to be large enough. If $c$ is well below the true effect, as in a large trial, most estimates clear it anyway and the selection makes little difference. If $c$ is above the true effect, as in a small trial, an estimate can only clear it if chance has pushed it upwards. The significant results from small trials will then be too large on average.

We can work out by how much. For a normal variable, the average value given that it exceeds a threshold is[^trunc]

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat\delta \;\big|\; \hat\delta > c\big] = \delta + \mathrm{SE} \cdot \frac{\phi(a)}{1 - \Phi(a)}, \qquad a = \frac{c - \delta}{\mathrm{SE}} = 1.96 - \frac{\delta}{\mathrm{SE}},
$$

where $\phi$ is the standard normal density. The second term is the average amount by which significant estimates overshoot. It gets larger as $a$ gets larger, which happens as the trial gets smaller. Dividing the average significant estimate by the true effect gives an exaggeration ratio. For our example:

| Patients per arm | $\delta/\mathrm{SE}$ | Power | Smallest significant difference | Average significant estimate | Exaggeration |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.49 | 8% | 7.9 points | 9.7 points | 4.9× |
| 200 | 0.70 | 11% | 5.6 points | 7.0 points | 3.5× |
| 500 | 1.11 | 20% | 3.6 points | 4.6 points | 2.3× |
| 1,000 | 1.56 | 35% | 2.5 points | 3.4 points | 1.7× |
| 2,000 | 2.21 | 60% | 1.8 points | 2.6 points | 1.3× |
| 3,210 | 2.80 | 80% | 1.4 points | 2.2 points | 1.1× |
| 5,000 | 3.50 | 94% | 1.1 points | 2.1 points | 1.0× |

With 200 patients per arm, a significant trial reports a risk difference of about 7 percentage points on average, when the true difference is 2. Each of these trials could have been run and analysed correctly. The overestimate comes from the fact that we only see a large effect when the trial is significant, and in a small trial the trial is only significant when the effect is overestimated.

Small trials can also be significant in the wrong direction. With 200 per arm, about 4% of significant results suggest the drug causes strokes; with 100 per arm, about 9%. With adequate power this almost never happens.

This gives one explanation for something often seen in practice. The first small studies of a treatment tend to report larger effects than the larger trials that follow. Some of this will be due to differences in patients or methods, but some of it is expected from the arithmetic above, even if every study is done properly. It also means that pooling small studies does not fully solve the problem if only the significant ones were published, since each of them is likely to be an overestimate.

To summarise. The error in an estimated difference falls with the square root of the sample size. Power depends on the size of the true effect relative to that error, and the sample size needed for a given power is proportional to one over the effect squared. A non-significant result from an underpowered trial is weak evidence that there is no effect. A significant result from an underpowered trial is likely to overstate the effect, and the amount can be calculated.

[^var]: Each observed proportion $\hat p_i$ is the mean of $n$ independent 0/1 outcomes, each with variance $p_i(1-p_i)$, so $\operatorname{Var}(\hat p_i) = p_i(1-p_i)/n$. The arms are independent, so the variance of the difference is the sum of the two. The normal approximation comes from the central limit theorem and is reasonable when neither arm has very few events.

[^tail]: A two-sided test is also significant if $\hat\delta < -c$, so the exact power is $\Phi(\delta/\mathrm{SE} - 1.96) + \Phi(-\delta/\mathrm{SE} - 1.96)$. The second term is the chance of a significant result in the wrong direction. It is tiny except in very small trials.

[^trunc]: Let $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and $a = (c-\mu)/\sigma$. Writing $X = \mu + \sigma Z$ with $Z$ standard normal, $\mathbb{E}[X \mid X > c] = \mu + \sigma\,\mathbb{E}[Z \mid Z > a]$. Now $\mathbb{E}[Z \mid Z > a] = \int_a^\infty z\,\phi(z)\,dz \,/\, (1-\Phi(a))$, and since $\phi'(z) = -z\,\phi(z)$ the integral is $\phi(a)$. The table applies this to trials that are significant in favour of the drug.
